analysis.one_liner: Bans seclusion and dangerous restraints of students in federally funded schools.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 11, 2025 with 51 cosponsors, including 1 Republican, and was referred to two House committees; no committee action has been taken since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban schools and Head Start programs that get federal money from locking students alone in rooms they cannot leave (seclusion), and from using mechanical restraints, drugs to control behavior, or physical holds that restrict breathing. Physical restraint would be allowed only when a student poses an imminent danger of serious physical injury, and only by trained staff. Parents would have to be notified the same day after any restraint incident, states would have to report restraint data publicly, and students or parents could sue programs that violate the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Students, especially students with disabilities who are subjected to seclusion and restraint far more often than other students, along with their parents, who would get same-day notification after any restraint incident and a private right to sue over violations. School staff would get federally funded training in de-escalation and positive behavioral interventions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits seclusion — involuntarily confining a student alone in a room from which they are physically prevented from leaving — in any program that receives federal financial assistance [S2][S3].

It bans mechanical restraints, chemical restraints (drugs used to control behavior rather than treat a diagnosed condition), and physical restraints that restrict breathing or are life threatening, including prone and supine holds [S2][S3].

Any allowed physical restraint must respond to an imminent danger of serious physical injury, use the least force necessary, and end as soon as the danger stops; the student must not be prevented from communicating [S3].

Parents must get same-day verbal or electronic notice and written notification within 24 hours after a restraint incident, plus a meeting with school staff within 5 school days to plan how to prevent a repeat [S3].

States must publicly report restraint data broken down by race, disability status, economic disadvantage, and school type, and students or parents can sue programs that use unlawful seclusion or restraint; the departments of Education and Health and Human Services must withhold federal payments from programs that violate the law [S2][S3].

The bill authorizes $40 million per year for fiscal 2026 through 2030 in grants to state education agencies for staff training, data collection, and positive behavioral interventions and supports [S3].

analysis.who_pays: School districts and Head Start programs, which would bear the cost of training and certifying staff, reporting data, and potential lawsuits under the new private right of action. Programs found in violation could have federal payments withheld, and private special education schools serving students who receive federal special education services are covered too.
analysis.who_pays_short: School districts and Head Start programs

drawbacks.text: Schools would face real compliance costs: every state must ensure enough staff are trained and certified through a state-approved crisis intervention program, and programs must set up parent-notification and post-incident meeting procedures after every restraint [S2][S3].

The private right of action, with attorneys' fees available to plaintiffs and no Eleventh Amendment immunity, exposes school districts to civil lawsuits from families, which school groups could reasonably argue will drive defensive litigation rather than better practices [S3].
The penalty of withholding federal payments falls partly on the students themselves, since cutting a program's federal funding reduces the money available to serve children in it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are significant: seclusion and breathing-restricting restraints have injured and killed students, and the families most affected are those of children with disabilities. The costs are genuine but ordinary for a federal education mandate — staff training, paperwork, and litigation risk — and the bill includes funding to help states train staff. The funding-withholding penalty is the weakest design element because it can hurt the students it is meant to protect. On balance, the help to students outweighs the compliance burden, though the bill is only at the first step of the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-December 2025 and referred to the Education and Workforce and Armed Services committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Beyer introduced the bill in the House on December 11, 2025 [S1][S5].

It was referred to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to the Committee on Armed Services; the Armed Services referral covers the bill's section on Department of Defense schools [S3][S5].
The bill has 51 cosponsors — 50 House Democrats and 1 Republican, Rep. Hamadeh of Arizona — and no action has been taken beyond the original referral [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won anything yet; the current rules, which allow seclusion and restraint under federal civil rights guidance rather than a statutory ban, remain in place while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current rules remain

for.name: Rep. Abraham Hamadeh
for.role: U.S. Representative, AZ-8; the bill's only Republican cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: Support is almost entirely Democratic — 50 of the 51 cosponsors are Democrats, with a single Republican, Rep. Hamadeh of Arizona, joining the sponsor — and no Republican has acted against the bill on record yet; it simply has not moved.

industries.industry: Public school districts and Head Start programs
industries.note: The bill imposes training, reporting, and litigation obligations on them and allows federal payments to be withheld for violations, but also sends grant money their way for de-escalation training and positive behavioral supports. Their interest in avoiding lawsuits and penalties is not aligned with students' interest in protection from seclusion and restraint.

industries.industry: Private special education schools serving federally funded special education students
industries.note: Private schools are covered if they enroll students who receive federal special education services, so they face the same prohibition on seclusion and limits on restraint, but private schools that receive no federal support are left untouched [S3].

industries.industry: Crisis intervention and de-escalation training providers
industries.note: Every state would need a state-approved crisis intervention training program certifying school staff, creating demand for these services; the federal grant program pays for the training.

analysis.trajectory: A late-session introduction with two committee referrals and 51 cosponsors in a chamber of 435 members almost never advances without a committee decision to move it; absent an unusual push by House leadership or a committee hearing, the bill is likely to die in committee at the end of this Congress.
